method: Every one of the 71 locks the raw detector places on a human-labelled no-ball frame was viewed as a 140 px crop with the lock cross-haired. Ambiguous cases were re-cut at 64 px and, where that was still not decisive, checked against consecutive source frames from the video to see whether the object moved.

classes.racquet: racquet head, frame, throat or grip. Ball-sized, often ball-coloured, MOVES on an arc.
classes.held_ball: a real ball not in play - held in the hand, resting on the strings, or sitting in a courtside basket.
classes.court_surface: plain court with no feature at the lock.
classes.fence: fence, windscreen, netting behind the court.
classes.net: net cord, tape, post, or equipment sitting against the net.
classes.background: trees, buildings, spectators, anything off the court.

corrections: A first pass read the am_hard_utr cluster at x~990-1001, y~488-502 as balls lying on the court by the net. That was WRONG. corrections_2026_08_11: gold_uR5q2cSM6AY was promoted to gold on the argument that it is a full SwingVision export — mini-court radar, speed readout, tennis-ball logo — and would therefore test a confuser regime nothing else in the exam set covered. It scored the HIGHEST raw false fire in the set (46.9%, 15 of 32 no-ball frames), which read as confirmation. Viewing all 15 REFUTES it: none is on a burned-in graphic. Eleven are the racquet head, two the player's white shoes, two white court marks. The clip tests the ordinary person-attached confuser — harder than average because a 3.3 m mount puts a large player in frame — not the overlay. The prediction was wrong and the clip is still worth having, for a different reason than the one it was chosen for.
